desc:
A marble is dropped into a rectangular grid in which 0 marks a free cell and 1 marks a blocked cell. It may start in any free cell of the top row. On every step it falls to the next row, landing in the cell directly below, the cell below and to the left, or the cell below and to the right (never leaving the grid, never entering a blocked cell). It stops when it reaches the bottom row.

Count the different falls, where two falls differ when they visit different cells. Because the count can be large, return it modulo 1,000,000,007.

grid = [[0,0,0],
        [0,1,0],
        [0,0,0]]   ->  8
grid = [[0,1,0],
        [1,0,1]]   ->  2

In the first example the marble has 2 ways to reach each of the two free cells of the middle row next to the block, and these extend to 2 + 4 + 2 ways in the bottom row.
constraints: If the grid has a single row, every free cell counts as one fall of length zero
hints: Look only at the last cell of a fall. In which cells of the previous row could the marble have been one step earlier?
Let ways[r][c] be the number of falls that end in cell (r, c). A blocked cell has 0 ways; a free cell adds up the ways of up to three cells in the row above.
Seed the top row with 1 for every free cell, then fill row by row. Only the previous row is needed. Reduce modulo 1,000,000,007 as you go, and sum the bottom row at the end.
editorial: Count falls cell by cell. Every fall that ends in the free cell (r, c) with r > 0 came from (r-1, c-1), (r-1, c) or (r-1, c+1), and the falls arriving through different predecessors are different. So ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c-1] + ways[r-1][c] + ways[r-1][c+1] (ignoring neighbours outside the grid), and a blocked cell is forced to 0, which stops any fall from passing through it.

The top row is the base: a free cell starts exactly one fall. The answer is the sum of ways over the bottom row. Because each row depends only on the row above, two arrays of width n suffice. Time O(m · n), extra space O(n). Taking the remainder after every cell keeps numbers small.
